title: Thales: The First Greek Thinker Who Saw Water Everywhere
hook: Imagine a trader from a bustling port town who stopped asking gods why the sky is blue and started looking for a natural answer.

sections.heading: A Mercantile Kid from Miletus
paragraphs: Thales was born around 625 BC in Miletus, a busy trading city on the western coast of what is now Turkey. The town sat at the mouth of the Maeander River, so ships came and went like the traffic on the N1 highway today. His family was well‑off – ancient writers say he came from a noble line, though they disagree whether his ancestors were Greek, Phoenician or a mix.

We don’t have a biography written by Thales himself. The main story we get comes from Diogenes Laërtius, a third‑century AD writer who collected old anecdotes. Because Diogenes wrote centuries after Thales died, some details are fuzzy, but they give us a picture of a curious young man who loved the sea, numbers and the sky.

sections.heading: Two Moments That Made History
paragraphs: One story that survived is Thales’ prediction of a solar eclipse in 585 BC. The Greek historian Herodotus says the eclipse happened just as the Lydian king Alyattes was fighting the Medes, and the sudden darkening stopped the battle. Whether Thales really calculated the date or simply noticed a pattern is debated, but the tale shows he was the first to try a scientific explanation for a celestial event.

Another famous episode is his engineering trick for the Lydian army. Supposedly, Thales showed the soldiers how to float a heavy wooden bridge over the Halys River by using a raft made of tightly bound logs. The story illustrates his belief that natural principles – in this case buoyancy – could solve practical problems, turning philosophy into a tool for everyday life.

sections.heading: What He Said About the World
paragraphs: Thales argued that everything in nature comes from a single underlying substance. He chose water because he saw it in rivers, rain, and even in the moisture that makes plants grow. To picture this, think of a South African braai where the fire is the visible part, but the heat that cooks the meat actually comes from the invisible gas that fuels the flames. For Thales, water was the invisible “fuel” behind all things.

He also claimed the Earth floated on water, like a wooden log on a pond. This may sound odd now, but it was a bold move away from mythic explanations that blamed the gods for every rock and river. By looking for a natural, material cause, Thales set the stage for later scientists who would ask “what is the thing that holds everything together?”

sections.heading: His Ideas in Today’s World
paragraphs: The notion of a single underlying principle lives on in modern physics. Scientists search for a “theory of everything” that would unite gravity, electromagnetism and the forces inside atoms – a 21st‑century echo of Thales’ water. Even the simple geometry he used, like the theorem that a triangle inscribed in a circle has a right angle, is taught in every school maths class.

In everyday life, Thales’ habit of looking for natural explanations shows up when we check the weather forecast instead of just assuming it will rain because “the gods are angry”. Load‑shedding schedules, for example, are based on calculations of electricity demand and supply, a direct descendant of the kind of practical reasoning Thales championed.

sections.heading: Why He Still Matters
paragraphs: Thales is counted among the Seven Sages, a group of wise men whose sayings still appear on the walls of the ancient Temple of Apollo at Delphi. His maxim “know thyself” reminds us that philosophy starts with asking simple questions about who we are and how the world works.

Even though we can’t be sure how many of the stories about him are true, the impact is clear: he moved philosophy from myth‑talk to observation, measurement and deduction. That shift is the foundation of science, engineering and the critical thinking we use when we decide whether to bring an extra kettle during load‑shedding.

guess.q: What natural phenomenon is Thales famously said to have predicted?
guess.explain: Ancient sources credit Thales with foretelling a solar eclipse that halted a battle, marking one of the earliest recorded attempts at astronomical prediction.

bigNumber.label: Year of the eclipse Thales allegedly predicted, stopping a war.

mythFact.myth: Thales was the first person ever to think about nature.
mythFact.fact: He was the first known Greek to replace myth with natural explanations, but earlier thinkers in Egypt and Babylon also studied nature.

didYouKnow: Plutarch wrote that Thales was the only one of his time to turn philosophy from mere speculation into practical activity.
rememberIt: Thales taught us to look for a single natural cause behind everything, even if that cause is just water.

recall.a: In the coastal city of Miletus, in ancient Ionia.

recall.q: What single substance did Thales think made up everything?
recall.a: He believed water was the fundamental substance.

recall.q: Which ancient event is linked to Thales’ eclipse prediction?
recall.a: A battle between the Lydians and the Medes in 585 BC.
